To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of bedside behavioral scales and electrophysiology can help us to distinguish between patients who are conscious and those who are unconscious.

(a) the diagnosis of the state of consciousness is based on behavioral observations, and that (b) electrophysiological and neuroimaging methods can help in understanding residual brain function and its relation to the level of consciousness.

the diagnosis and prognosis of disorders of consciousness are difficult, that the use of behavioral evaluation scales is important, and that the use of functional neuroimaging techniques can provide additional diagnostic information.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the residual brain function and the quality of life in disorders of consciousness and aims to improve the diagnosis, prognosis and therapy of these patients.
the study of residual brain function in patients with disorders of consciousness, and with the development of diagnostic tools to improve the clinical evaluation and the treatment of these patients.
the residual brain function in patients who have survived an acute brain damage and remain in a coma or vegetative state (VS).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the diagnosis and prognosis of disorders of consciousness are not yet as reliable as we would like them to be, that the current diagnostic tools have to be improved and that the ethical issues of these patients have to be further explored.
the diagnosis of the level of consciousness in patients who are in a coma, a vegetative state, a minimally conscious state, or a locked-in syndrome is still a challenging issue.

there is still no conclusive evidence for a residual brain function in these disorders, but there are some indications for residual brain activity in patients who survive an ischemic stroke, and in patients with locked-in syndrome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to detect residual brain function in the majority of comatose patients.
residual brain function in disorders of consciousness is more widespread than previously thought, but the exact mechanisms and brain regions involved remain to be clarified.
the residual brain function in patients in coma or in a vegetative state is more extensive and complex than previously thought, but that it is still limited compared to that of healthy subjects.
The main takeaway from our work is that

residual brain function is preserved in most patients with disorders of consciousness and that the use of behavioral, electrophysiological and functional imaging tools in combination can help to identify and better characterize this residual brain function.

residual brain function in patients with disorders of consciousness can be studied with electrophysiology or neuroimaging, and that this can help to identify patients who are awake, aware, or have the ability to communicate, and who therefore may benefit from rehabilitative therapy.
the residual brain function in patients in coma and related disorders is more complex than previously thought.
